items.requirement: The service must isolate each customer company's fleet, sites, charging pads, jobs, flights, and operational problems so that users of one customer company cannot view or modify another customer company's data.
The service must prevent the airspace desk from viewing or accessing any individual customer company's fleet, sites, charging pads, jobs, flights, or operational problems.
The service must share airspace information—including flight corridors, zones, prohibited flying areas, and authority closures—across all customer companies.
The service must allow a company to register and manage its own named sites, including the maximum number of drones that can take off and land at each site at the same time.
The service must allow a fleet technician to set up charging pads at their company's sites and record each charging pad's charging connector type.
The service must restrict each charging pad exclusively to the owning company's drones and must never assign or lend a company's charging pad to another company's drone.

The service must store drone model specifications across multiple manufacturers, including carrying capacity, flight range on a full battery, carried sensors (such as cameras, thermal cameras, and laser scanners), and charging connector type, so that eachcompany can manage a fleet of hundreds of drones and dozens of charging pads.
The service must allow a fleet technician to add a new drone to their company's fleet with its model and assigned home site, and to retire a drone from the fleet so it can no longer be dispatched.

The service must allow a fleet technician to take a drone out of service for repairs or servicing—preventing it from being dispatched while out of service—and to return the drone to service once fixed.
The service must record all repairs, servicing, and status history for each drone so that the operating company can present maintenance records to regulators upon request.
The service must allow a fleet technician to send a drone to charge only at a charging pad owned by the same company that has a matching, compatible charging connector type.
The service must support planning and dispatching delivery jobs that carry a specified load from an origin site to a destination site.
The service must support planning and dispatching inspection jobs that require a drone equipped with specified sensors to visit an ordered list of points and return to the starting site.

When a dispatcher is planning a job, the service must identify which of the company's available, in-service drones can reach the job's starting site and meet the job's load capacity, sensor, range, and charging connector constraints.
The service must never automatically select a drone or a flight path for a job; a dispatcher must explicitly choose both the drone and the sequence of flight corridors it will fly.
The service must require a dispatcher to explicitly sign off a flight plan—recording the responsible dispatcher's sign-off—before the drone is permitted to depart.

When multiple dispatchers plan and sign off flights concurrently, the service must prevent the same drone from being assigned to overlapping flights and must prevent any site's simultaneous take-off and landing limit from being exceeded.
The service must prevent a dispatcher from signing off a flight whose chosen path passes through a prohibited zone or an airspace closure that is active during the flight.
The service must allow a dispatcher to call off any of their company's flights before departure or while the drone is in the air.

The service must accept and record reports from people and devices outside the company indicating whether a delivery load is ready, whether a drone has reached each ordered point of its job, and whether a drone has arrived at its destination.

The service must tolerate drone relay reports and external reports arriving late, out of order, more than once, or not at all—deduplicating repeated reports, ordering events accurately, and surfacing missing expected reports without corrupting flight or battery status.

The service must track reported in-flight battery drain—including faster-than-planned drain caused by cold or wind—and allow a flight to continue seamlessly when a drone restarts in flight after a software fault.

The service must ensure that instructions sent to drones and charging equipment are idempotent and trackable across retries so that lost acknowledgments or duplicate deliveries do not trigger unintended repeated actions.
The service must allow the airspace desk to create and update the shared network of flight corridors between named sites and the zones that group corridors or define areas where flying is prohibited.
The service must allow the airspace desk to enter planned airspace closures with a start and end time, as well as sudden closures that take effect immediately.
The service must allow the airspace desk to amend an existing airspace closure—including widening its area or changing its end time—even while drones from multiple companies are in the air.

When a closure comes into force or is amended, the service must immediately identify and notify each affected company's dispatchers of any signed-off or in-flight flights belonging to their company that intersect the affected airspace.

When an airspace closure is entered or amended, the service must display to the airspace desk an aggregate measure of the disruption caused across all customer companies without revealing any individual company's flights, jobs, fleet, or sites.

The service must persist all fleet, charging pad, site, job, active flight, sign-off, and airspace state so that after a software update, restart, or crash during working hours, the service recovers within a few minutes without losing state for drones already in the air.
